text: InvestCloud Cuts 150+ Jobs in 2026: CEO Jeff Yabuki Cites AI Skip to content InvestCloud Cuts 150+ Jobs In Digital Wealth Division In 2026: CEO Jeff Yabuki Cites AI-Driven Restructuring Craig Iskowitz March 9, 2026 Key Facts Company: InvestCloud (backed by Motive Partners) CEO: Jeff Yabuki Jobs cut: 150+ positions Division affected: Digital Wealth Primary reasons cited: AI productivity gains, geographic dispersal, shift to productized innovation No layoffs in: APL Managed Accounts Platform, Private Markets Network Every technology revolution has a tipping point. That moment when the new tech stops being just a strategy slide and starts impacting organizational structure. The wealthtech space reached this point on Monday. In an exclusive interview, WealthTech Today sat down with Jeff Yabuki, CEO of InvestCloud, backed by private equity firm Motive Partners, to explain why the wealthtech giant will eliminate more than 150 positions within its Digital Wealth division. According to an internal communication from Yabuki distributed to all InvestCloud employees and reviewed by WealthTech Today on Monday, March 9, the CEO cites three converging forces: accelerating AI productivity and time-to-market gains, geographic dispersal that has hampered scale, and a strategic shift away from bespoke client solutions toward productized, repeatable innovation. InvestCloud joins a growing roster of financial services firms — and more than 45 companies across industries — that have explicitly named AI as a driver of workforce reductions. Since early 2025, that trend has already displaced more than 130,000 workers globally, according to tracking by Programs.com. “We have seen the rate of technological change accelerate exponentially even since launching our new strategy,” Yabuki wrote in the communication. Notably, the cuts will not touch the company’s APL managed accounts business or its Private Markets Network. Yabuki views both as engines of future growth without the structural issues the company is addressing in the Digital Wealth business, and he anticipates AI will play a very important role in this industry trend as well. InvestCloud returned to positive revenue growth in 2025, one year ahead of the schedule Yabuki had set when he took the helm. That is the good news. The harder truth is that the same AI wave lifting the company’s strategic ambitions is also doing something no executive likes to announce: making a significant portion of its current workforce redundant. Why InvestCloud Is Cutting Jobs: Three Pillars of the AI Restructuring Yabuki framed the restructuring around three pillars. First, InvestCloud intends to elevate what it calls its “SMART” intelligent capabilities, leveraging connected data and building an agentic ecosystem across both its advisor and investor experience platforms. Second, AI-driven productivity gains will allow the company to stop building one-off custom solutions for individual clients, shifting instead toward standardized products that deploy faster and more consistently. Third — and this one carries the most organizational weight — it will consolidate its geographically dispersed Digital Wealth operations into fewer, more concentrated centers of excellence. That last point deserves some unpacking. Geographic dispersion is a persistent challenge for software companies that have grown through acquisition, and InvestCloud is no exception. When talent and product teams are scattered across multiple countries and time zones, the economies of scale that AI promises can become harder to capture without consolidation. Layoffs are commonly part of the price of consolidation. Yabuki has been candid about this direction. In a February 2025 WealthTech Today podcast episode, he laid out his philosophy in terms that now read almost as advance notice of Monday’s announcement. “Innovation has to be industrialized,” he said. “It has to make a difference. A lot of times, innovations are created that aren’t able to scale.” The cuts in the Digital Wealth division seem to be a direct expression of that belief applied to the company’s own business. InvestCloud Joins Wave of AI Layoffs Hitting Block, BlackRock, and Goldman Sachs If this story feels familiar, it should. InvestCloud’s announcement lands against a backdrop of AI-driven workforce reductions that has been accelerating for over a year and shows no signs of slowing. The numbers are striking. According to a March 2026 analysis by Programs.com, which tracked company disclosures, earnings calls, and major media reporting, over 100,000 employees were impacted by AI-driven layoffs in 2025 alone. In just the first two months of 2026, that figure has already surpassed 30,000. More than 45 CEOs have explicitly cited AI efficiency as a driver of headcount reductions. The layoffs have spread well beyond Silicon Valley into finance, logistics, consulting, media, and manufacturing. The most dramatic recent example came from fintech. Block, the payments company led by Jack Dorsey, announced in late February that it was cutting more than 4,000 employees — nearly 40 percent of its workforce. Dorsey was blunt about the reason. “Intelligence tools have changed what it means to build and run a company,” he wrote in a shareholder letter. “A significantly smaller team, using the tools we’re building, can do more and do it better.” Investors cheered. Block’s stock soared more than 20 percent in premarket trading on the news. Block represents the most explicit public acknowledgment of AI as a workforce reduction driver. But it is hardly alone in financial services. BlackRock conducted two rounds of layoffs in 2025, cutting roughly 500 positions as it shifted resources toward technology and data-driven systems. The asset management giant has been expanding its use of AI across investment analysis and back-office operations, and some traditional support roles have simply disappeared in the process. Goldman Sachs signaled in an October 2025 internal memo — quickly picked up by Reuters — that job cuts and a hiring slowdown were coming as the firm pushed to capture AI productivity gains. The memo, signed by CEO David Solomon, President John Waldron, and CFO Denis Coleman, introduced an initiative dubbed “OneGS 3.0.” The bank’s leadership expressed confidence that AI gains would allow the firm to “re-invest those gains to continue delivering world-class solutions for clients.” It is a formulation that has become something of a corporate mantra in 2025 and 2026 — reassuring to shareholders, less so to anyone whose job sits in the path of the efficiency curve. The pattern holds across industries far beyond financial services. At least eight companies announced AI-related layoffs affecting more than 10,000 employees each in 2025 and early 2026, including Accenture, Amazon, Citigroup, and Microsoft. Salesforce cut 4,000 customer support roles after deploying AI agents that now handle roughly half of all customer interactions. Klarna’s CEO announced that AI was already doing the work of hundreds of employees. IBM said AI agents had replaced hundreds of back-office roles. These are not isolated incidents. They are the early chapters of a structural shift in how companies think about labor and automation — and wealthtech is no longer watching from the sidelines. What the InvestCloud Layoffs Don’t Touch: APL Platform and Private Markets Network What makes InvestCloud’s announcement distinct is the precision of the surgical strike. Yabuki is aggressively restructuring its Digital Wealth business, while explicitly protecting the company’s two highest-growth businesses. The APL managed accounts platform — one of the largest of its kind in the country, supporting nearly $4 trillion in assets across 10 million accounts — is untouched including industrializing alternative investment access across managed accounts through a new Private Markets Account sleeve structure. That initiative is now a central strategic bet. Yabuki has described it as analogous to the creation of payment networks like Visa and Mastercard — a common infrastructure, open to all participants, that creates confidence and velocity through standardization rather than competition. The logic is straightforward. Wealth management’s $30 trillion market currently has minimal exposure to private markets investments. The opportunity to build the infrastructure that standardizes and scales alternatives distribution is enormous. That work requires people with specialized skills. The Digital Wealth division, by contrast, has been doing expensive, bespoke implementation work that AI can increasingly replicate or replace. Consider firms like Buckingham Strategic Wealth, which partnered with InvestCloud to build a consolidated advisor and client experience portal, pulling data from Salesforce, MoneyGuidePro, Orion, and Plaid into a single interface. For clients like that, Monday’s announcement raises real questions. Will implementation timelines stretch? Will client service quality hold? According to Yabuki, in addition to accelerating its growth plan, the company has dramatically enhanced client quality and satisfaction, as referenceability is up exponentially – and now at a level the CEO has not seen in his prior leadership experiences. For wealth management technology specifically, the implications go beyond any single company’s headcount. Vendors are reconfiguring around AI in ways that will change what products get built, how quickly implementations are completed, and which capabilities attract investment. The business of wealth management technology is being reorganized in real time, and Yabuki intends for InvestCloud to benefit sooner rather than later. Every wealthtech vendor will eventually face this tipping point as AI reshapes how the industry operates. The question is which CEOs move decisively enough to lead that change, and which ones hesitate long enough to become the next casualty. Yabuki’s internal communication promises that the changes will “expand our capacity to innovate” and “further strengthen our ability to serve clients with excellence.” He also noted that client satisfaction and referenceability have risen significantly during the company’s turnaround.
